newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Germany postpones cut in solidarity tax.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Germany postpones cut in solidarity tax.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition avoided the political pitfall of raising petrol taxes but only at the cost of delaying a planned cut in the unpopular solidarity surcharge, coalition officials said on Friday.

Before coalition talks on Friday, Finance Minister Theo Waigel said there was little room to cut spending further to bridge a 1997 budget gap that widened this week by about 10 billion marks ($6.5 billion).
But German taxpayers made clear they would hold the coalition to its promises to lower taxes.

Kohl's junior coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP), which have made a name with anti-tax slogans, tried to put the best face on the matter by stressing that the bargain hammered out by coalition leaders on Friday included no tax increasses.
"There are no tax increases," FDP chairman Wolfgang Gerhardt told a news conference.

Instead, the government agreed not reduce the unpopular solidarity tax -- imposed to help finance the reconstruction of formerly communist east Germany -- which was to have been cut to 6.5 percent from the current 7.5 percent from January 1.

The spending gap appeared this week because of decisions to allow a wealth tax to lapse and to raise child allowances. The changes took effect automatically after Waigel and the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) failed to agree on the 1997 tax bill.
The SPD has the power to veto government tax measures through its control of the Bundesrat upper house of parliament.
Reports this week that the government was considering an increase in the petroleum tax sparked widespread protest from opposition parties, business associations and taxpayer groups.

The conservative daily Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung said Waigel was under pressure to bring Germany's budget in line with the Maastricht criteria for the single European currency, but that raising taxes was the wrong way to go.
Germans are better prepared to tolerate more government austerity than to pay ever higher taxes, the newspaper said.
"There has to be an end to this now," it said in an editorial.
The government had considered raising the petroleum tax up to 10 pfennigs a litre -- a measure which could have boosted revenues by an estimated seven billion marks.
The Taxpayers' Alliance strongly opposed the move.
"Citizens and enterprises are already suffering under an excessive burden of taxes and other withholdings," the alliance said in a statement.
Further reductions should be made in subsidies to east Germany and government personnel costs so taxes do not need to be raised, the alliance said.

The Bundesbank said on Thursday that subsidies to the east, which have totalled 615 billion marks since unification in 1990, were too high and should be reduced. Most of the money ends up financing consumption instead of investment, it said in its October monthly report. ($1=1.5423 Mark)
